name: postmodern dance

narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

instructor.persona: a patient, precise instructor who counts out loud, demonstrates from the front and the back, repeats every step slowly three times before speeding up, names mistakes kindly and never rushes
instructor.rule: counts out loud; demonstrates front and back; three slow repetitions before tempo; one correction at a time

scenes.title: Cold open
narration: Postmodern dance stripped away the proscenium stage and virtuosic technique, asserting that walking, sitting, or standing could be as valid a performance as the most complex balletic leap.
This is postmodern dance. 20th century.
on_screen: Hero video — MISSING
Title card: postmodern dance · United States · 20th century

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The movement originated in the early 1960s as a reaction against the rigidity of modern dance.
The Judson Dance Theater in New York City is credited as a primary pioneer, fostering an environment where avant-garde artists could experiment with unconventional methods.
on_screen: Map: United States · Global
Image — MISSING

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The movement served as a critique of the artistic process, often incorporating political themes related to censorship, war, and social justice.
It aimed to challenge audience expectations and the 'death of the author' in choreography.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Technique involves the use of pedestrian movement, improvisation, and spontaneous determination.
Choreographers often cast non-trained dancers to ensure authenticity and neutrality.
Movement is not bound to musical tempo but to objective clock-time.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music is often minimalist or nonexistent.
When present, it is frequently severed from the dance, with both operating by their own internal logic rather than synchronizing.

music_brief.purpose: original soundtrack faithful to the tradition, with documented commercial reuse rights and no recurring royalties
music_brief.rights_rule: A composition brief does not clear an output. Record the provider/model/version, terms and date, input rights, output licence, restrictions and review before release.
music_brief.prompt: Original instrumental composition in the musical world of postmodern dance (United States). New melody, new arrangement: do not quote or imitate any specific recorded song; keep the idiom, the instruments, the pulse and the proportions.

tracks.use: chapters: dance it to the music

rules: Original composition only — no sampling, no melody of any existing recording, no lyrics from any song.
Traditional public-domain tunes may be used only when the profile names them and a public-domain source is on file; otherwise compose new material in the idiom.
Keep the proportions true: the meter, the tempo range and the instrument roles the sources describe.
Label every generated track with the tool, the date and this brief, so provenance is always clear.

wardrobe.policy: neutral dress with a respectful nod (palette and fabric only): the sources describe sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire, or the dance is sacred
wardrobe.from_sources: Performances are often stripped down, featuring simple, casual costumes. The setting is not restricted to the proscenium stage and may occur in unconventional spaces.
care: every element traceable to the costume notes or a licensed image; nothing added for effect
no caricature, no exaggeration, no mixing of regions or eras
a culture bearer reviews the wardrobe before production; the review is recorded in the pack
credits name the tradition and the sources of the reconstruction

visual_brief.costume_notes: Performances are often stripped down, featuring simple, casual costumes. The setting is not restricted to the proscenium stage and may occur in unconventional spaces.
visual_brief.setting_notes: The movement served as a critique of the artistic process, often incorporating political themes related to censorship, war, and social justice. It aimed to challenge audience expectations and the 'death of the author' in choreography.
generation_rules: Generated imagery reconstructs costume and setting ONLY from the costume notes above and the licensed images; it is labelled 'reconstruction' on screen.
No likeness of a real, named person. No sacred objects or ceremonies beyond what the sources describe.
Licensed images and footage are shown with their attribution and licence text.

teaching_formula.source: 4 tutorial(s) of the stage-contemporary family studied
demonstration: views used by most teachers: front, mirror, back
cues: make a little bit space between feet
make some groovy in your chest
try to find in your spine
make the snake finish on your arms
short verbal cue the teacher repeats  8 words
hips to one side in little pulses
